stops.name: Massachusetts State House
stops.description: Charles Bulfinch finished this domed capitol in 1798 on pastureland John Hancock once used to graze cows, and the legislature has met here ever since.

stops.name: Beacon Hill Monument
stops.description: This column behind the State House marks the vanished summit of Beacon Hill, which was shovelled away in the early 1800s to fill in the Mill Pond.

stops.name: Boston Athenaeum
stops.description: One of the oldest independent libraries in the country, founded in 1807 and still run on paid memberships, with a half-number street address that trips up every delivery driver.

stops.name: Park Street Church
stops.description: The 217-foot steeple on this 1809 church was the first thing travellers saw approaching Boston, and William Lloyd Garrison gave his first antislavery speech inside it.

stops.name: Granary Burying Ground
stops.description: Paul Revere, Samuel Adams, John Hancock and the five men killed in the Boston Massacre are all buried in this 1660 graveyard, under about 2,300 markers for an estimated 5,000 burials.

stops.name: Brewer Fountain
stops.description: A 22-foot bronze fountain cast in Paris and given to the city in 1868, standing on Boston Common just above the Park Street subway entrance.

stops.name: King's Chapel
stops.description: Built of Quincy granite in 1754 as New England's first Anglican church, it became the first Unitarian congregation in America after the Revolution and still holds the country's oldest pulpit in use.

stops.name: King's Chapel Burying Ground
stops.description: Boston's oldest graveyard, opened in 1630, and older than the chapel it sits beside and takes its name from.

stops.name: Omni Parker House
stops.description: A hotel on this corner since 1855, where the Boston cream pie was invented and where Ho Chi Minh worked in the kitchen and Malcolm X bussed tables.

stops.name: Old City Hall
stops.description: Boston's city government sat in this 1865 mansard-roofed pile for a century, and it was one of the first French Second Empire buildings put up in the United States.

stops.name: Boston Irish Famine Memorial
stops.description: Two facing groups of statues on a small plaza, one starving in Ireland and one prospering in America, marking the famine years that remade this city.

stops.name: Old Corner Bookstore
stops.description: Built in 1718 as a house and apothecary, this corner became the publishing office where Hawthorne, Emerson and Longfellow were printed, and it is the oldest commercial building left downtown.

stops.name: Old South Meeting House
stops.description: Some 5,000 colonists packed this 1729 meeting house on the night of December 16, 1773, then walked out and threw the tea into the harbor.

stops.name: Winthrop Building
stops.description: Boston's first steel-frame skyscraper, finished in 1894, and its narrow curved facade follows a cowpath-era property line rather than any grid.

stops.name: Ames Building
stops.description: Boston's first skyscraper at 196 feet, completed in 1889 with masonry walls nine feet thick at the base because steel framing had not reached the city yet.

note: Boston has never appeared in the visible nightly history (the clone is shallow, 53 commits back to 2026-07-29: Atlanta, Baltimore, Dallas, Cleveland, Denver), so it wins outright and is alphabetically first among the untouched US cities. All 15 stops are verified against their own Wikipedia articles, all carry coordinates, and they form a tight loop of roughly one mile: State House and Ashburton Park on Beacon Hill, down Park and Tremont past the Common, along School Street, then Washington Street to Water Street and back up Court Street. Three stops have no street address and therefore no ZIP, all for the same honest reason - they are objects on a plaza or a park rather than buildings with a house number: Beacon Hill Monument (Ashburton Park, off Bowdoin St; hmdb.org offers a derived postal address of 60 Ashburton Pl but I did not trust an auto-generated one), Brewer Fountain (on Boston Common near Park and Tremont), and the Boston Irish Famine Memorial (the plaza between Washington and School Sts). Every other address was taken from the stop's own article or, where the article gave only an intersection, from the NRHP row plus an independent source; the Granary's address is the Freedom Trail's 95 Tremont St rather than boston.gov's 120 Tremont St, which is the number of Suffolk Law across the street. ZIPs were looked up per stop, so 02133 for the State House and 02109 for the Winthrop Building are correct and not typos for the 02108 that covers the rest. Deliberately omitted: the Old State House and the Boston Massacre Site, which the project notes record as already being in the waypoints table. Other Freedom Trail sites here may already be in the table too - I do not read the database, so the page's In-table check is the authority. Dropped from the sweep: streets and squares (State St, School St, Scollay Square), demolished or vanished buildings (Province House, Hancock Manor, the First Town-House, Tremont House, dozens of 19th-century theatres), and articles about events or firms rather than places (the 1689 Boston revolt, the Great Fire of 1872, Jordan Marsh, Southworth & Hawes).
